tagline: The book of the wilderness: a people counted and ordered around God's presence refuses to trust him, dies in the desert, and leaves its children at the edge of the promised land.
overview:
Numbers picks up where Exodus and Leviticus leave off. Israel has been rescued from Egypt, has received the law at Mount Sinai, and has built the tabernacle, the portable tent where God dwells among them. Now the people must travel from Sinai to Canaan, the land God promised to Abraham. The trip should take weeks (Deuteronomy 1:2 counts it as eleven days from Horeb, another name for Sinai, to Kadesh-barnea). It takes almost forty years. The Hebrew title of the book, Bemidbar, means "in the wilderness", and that is where nearly all of it happens. The English title comes, through Latin, from the Greek translation of the Old Testament called the Septuagint, which named the book Arithmoi after the two counts of the people in chapters 1 and 26.

The book tells how a well-ordered camp became a generation of graves. It opens with the census, the arrangement of the tribes around the tabernacle, and the laws that keep the camp fit for God's presence. Then the march begins, and so do the complaints: about food, about Moses, and finally, when twelve scouts return from Canaan in chapters 13 and 14, about the land itself. The people refuse to go in, and God sentences that generation to die in the wilderness. Rebellions follow (Korah's challenge to Aaron's priesthood, Moses' own failure at the waters of Meribah), and yet God keeps providing water, food, guidance, and mercy. On the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, a foreign seer named Balaam is hired to curse Israel and can only bless it. A second census counts a new generation, and the book closes with preparations for entering the land: a new leader, Joshua; laws for offerings, vows, and inheritance; and borders drawn for a country Israel does not yet hold.

Numbers matters because it is honest about what happens after rescue. Freedom from Egypt did not make Israel trusting or grateful, and the book does not pretend otherwise. It shows a God who is holy and dangerous to approach carelessly, who judges unbelief, and who still refuses to abandon his promise. The New Testament returns to it again and again as a mirror for people who have been rescued and must now learn to trust.
author:
The book does not name its author, but Jewish and Christian tradition has long credited Moses with the five books of the Torah (the Pentateuch), Numbers among them. The book itself says that Moses recorded the stages of Israel's march at the LORD's command (33:2), and much of it is presented as God's speech to Moses. Traditional scholars hold that Moses is the source of the book's substance, while allowing for later editorial touches, such as the remark that Moses was the humblest man on earth (12:3), which reads more naturally as someone else's comment. The book also cites older writings, including a poem from "the Book of the Wars of the LORD" (21:14), showing that its writer drew on existing sources.

Most critical scholars since the nineteenth century have seen the Pentateuch as woven together from several written strands over a long period. On that view, much of Numbers (the lists, the camp arrangement, the priestly laws) belongs to a priestly source often dated to the exile or after it, combined with older narrative traditions about the wilderness. Some recent scholars place much of Numbers late in the Pentateuch's formation, as a bridge between the priestly material and Deuteronomy. The book's rough edges, such as laws set between stories and repeated episodes of water from a rock (Exodus 17 and Numbers 20), are read one way by those who see separate sources and another by those who see deliberate arrangement.
date:
The events run from the first day of the second month of the second year after the exodus (1:1) to the fortieth year (33:38), about thirty-eight years in all. When that was depends on the date of the exodus, which is debated. An earlier date, around 1446 BC, rests largely on 1 Kings 6:1, which puts the exodus 480 years before Solomon began the temple. A later date, in the thirteenth century BC, rests on the mention of the store city Rameses (Exodus 1:11) and on the archaeological picture of Canaan in that period. Some scholars doubt that the wilderness period can be dated at all.

The date of writing follows the question of authorship. Those who hold to Mosaic authorship place the book's substance at the end of the wilderness period, with some later editing. Critical scholars usually date the final form to the Persian period, after the return from Babylonian exile (after 539 BC), while granting that it contains older traditions, poems, and lists. Two archaeological finds bear on the age of the book's material without settling the question. Two tiny silver scrolls found at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem in 1979, dated to about the late seventh or early sixth century BC, carry a form of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24-26. And a plaster inscription found at Tell Deir Alla in Jordan in 1967, dated to about the eighth century BC, tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor, the same name as the prophet of Numbers 22 to 24.
setting:
Numbers moves through three places. It opens in the Wilderness of Sinai, where Israel has camped for about a year beneath the mountain of the law. It then crosses the dry country of the Sinai peninsula and the southern Negev, the Wilderness of Paran and the Wilderness of Zin, with Kadesh-barnea, an oasis region on the southern edge of Canaan, as the base for much of the forty years. Finally it moves east of the Dead Sea and north into the Transjordan, the highlands east of the Jordan River, and ends on the plains of Moab opposite Jericho.

The peoples Israel meets there were real neighbors throughout the rest of the Old Testament: Edom to the south of the Dead Sea (descended, in Genesis, from Jacob's brother Esau), Moab to its east (descended from Lot), the Amorite kingdoms of Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan north of Moab, and the Midianites, a desert people connected with Moses' own in-laws. Life in the camp was tribal. People belonged to a father's house, then a clan, then a tribe, and land, inheritance, military service, and worship were all organized that way. The first readers, whether they were Israelites in the land or exiles hoping to return to it, would have recognized themselves in a generation standing at the border, deciding whether to trust God with what lay ahead.
purpose: Numbers was written to show Israel who it was and what it had done. It records the ordering of the people around God's presence so that later generations would know how the camp, the priesthood, and the tribes were meant to fit together. It preserves the laws given along the way, many of them for life in the land still to come. Above all it tells the story of the wilderness generation as a warning and a comfort. The warning is that rescue does not guarantee arrival: a people can see God's power and still refuse to trust him, and that refusal has consequences. The comfort is that God's promise outlasts the people who reject it. The children of the rebels are counted, blessed, and led to the border, and the laws of chapters 27 to 36 are written in the confident expectation that Israel will soon live in the land. Every later generation of Israel, including those in exile, could read it as a question addressed to them: will you be the generation that trusts?
story: Numbers is the fourth book of the Bible and the fourth book of the Torah. Genesis tells of God's promise to Abraham of land, descendants, and blessing for all nations. Exodus tells of the rescue from Egypt, the covenant at Sinai (a binding agreement in which God commits himself to Israel and Israel to him), and the building of the tabernacle. Leviticus gives the laws of sacrifice, priesthood, and holiness that allow a holy God to live among a sinful people. Numbers takes that people out of Sinai and toward the land, and shows how badly the first generation handles the road. Deuteronomy follows, set on the same plains of Moab where Numbers ends: Moses' farewell sermons to the new generation before his death. Joshua then tells of the crossing of the Jordan and the entry into Canaan. Later Scripture keeps returning to the wilderness years, in the Psalms (Psalm 78, 95, and 106), in the prophets, and in the New Testament.
christ:
The New Testament reads Numbers as a story that concerns the church directly. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, recalls the cloud, the manna, the water from the rock, and the deaths in the desert, and says of the rock that "that rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4); he adds that "these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us" (1 Corinthians 10:11). The letter to the Hebrews warns its readers against repeating Kadesh-barnea: "it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter" (Hebrews 3:19). Jesus himself used the bronze serpent of Numbers 21 to explain his death: "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14).

Other lines run from the book to Christ without being predictions in the narrow sense. Aaron, running into the plague with incense and standing "between the living and the dead" (16:48), shows what a priest who intercedes for the guilty looks like. Moses asks God for a leader so that the people will not be "like sheep without a shepherd" (27:17), and the Gospels use the same picture of the crowds Jesus saw (Mark 6:34). The successor God gives is Joshua, whose name in Greek is the same as Jesus'. Balaam's vision of a star and a scepter rising from Israel (24:17) was read by later Jewish interpreters as a promise of a coming king, and Christians have read it of Christ. And where Israel spent forty years in the wilderness and failed its tests, the Gospels show Jesus spending forty days in the wilderness and remaining faithful.
reading:
Numbers mixes kinds of writing more than any other book of the Torah: census lists, camp diagrams in prose, laws, rituals, narratives, travel records, and poetry (the priestly blessing, the song of the well in 21:17-18, and Balaam's oracles). Modern readers are tempted to skip the lists and laws and read only the stories. It helps to notice how the book alternates between them. The laws are often placed where they answer the story around them: after the people refuse to enter the land in chapter 14, chapter 15 opens with laws that begin "After you enter the land" (15:2), a quiet promise that there will be a future.

Watch for the pattern of complaint, judgment, and intercession that repeats through chapters 11 to 21, and for the contrast between the first census (chapter 1) and the second (chapter 26), which frames the whole book as the passing of one generation and the rise of another. Dennis Olson's study The Death of the Old and the Birth of the New (1985) made this two-generation shape widely recognized. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. One is to treat the wilderness only as punishment, when the book is equally full of God's provision. The other is to read Balaam as either a simple villain or a simple hero; the book presents him as a seer who speaks God's words and later (31:16) as the source of the plot that led Israel into sin at Peor.

structure.title: The camp ordered at Sinai
structure.summary: The first census, the arrangement of the tribes around the tabernacle, the duties of the Levites, laws of purity and vows, the priestly blessing, the leaders' gifts, the second Passover, and the signals for the march.

structure.title: Setting out and the first complaints
structure.summary: Israel leaves Sinai following the cloud. The people complain at Taberah and crave meat at Kibroth-hattaavah, Moses is given seventy elders to share his burden, and Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses.

structure.title: The scouts and the refusal
structure.summary: Twelve scouts explore Canaan; ten report that it cannot be taken. The people refuse to go in, Moses intercedes, and God sentences the generation to forty years in the wilderness.

structure.title: Rebellion and the priesthood confirmed
structure.summary: Laws for life in the coming land, Korah's rebellion and its judgment, Aaron's budding staff, the duties and support of priests and Levites, and the ritual of the red heifer for cleansing from contact with death.

structure.title: The road to Moab
structure.summary: Miriam dies, Moses strikes the rock and is barred from the land, Edom refuses passage, and Aaron dies. After the bronze serpent, Israel defeats Sihon and Og and reaches the plains of Moab.

structure.title: Balaam and Baal of Peor
structure.summary: King Balak of Moab hires Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam can speak only blessing. Then Israel falls into idolatry and sexual sin with the Moabites and Midianites at Peor, and Phinehas stops the plague.

structure.title: The new generation on the plains of Moab
structure.summary: A second census counts the new generation. Laws follow for inheritance, offerings, and vows; Joshua is commissioned; Midian is punished; two and a half tribes settle east of the Jordan; and the borders, Levitical cities, and cities of refuge are set for the land ahead.

themes.title: God in the middle of the camp
themes.body: The book begins by arranging the whole people around the tabernacle, with the Levites nearest and the tribes on four sides. God's presence, seen in the cloud by day and fire by night, is the center of Israel's life and the guide for every move. That presence is a gift and a danger at once: the holy God cannot be approached carelessly, and much of Numbers is concerned with the boundaries, purifications, and priestly duties that let him live among an unholy people without destroying them.

themes.title: Complaint and unbelief
themes.body: From chapter 11 on, the people grumble about food, water, leadership, and the land itself. The complaints are more than bad temper. They amount to a rejection of the God who rescued them and a wish to return to Egypt. At Kadesh the refusal becomes final for that generation. Numbers treats unbelief not as a private doubt but as a turning away that shapes a whole community's future.

themes.title: Judgment and intercession
themes.body: God's judgments in Numbers are severe: fire, plague, the earth opening, serpents, and the sentence of death in the desert. Yet again and again someone stands in the gap. Moses pleads on the basis of God's own character and reputation, Aaron runs into the plague with incense, and Phinehas turns back God's anger. The book presents a God whose justice is real and whose mercy is moved by intercession.

themes.title: The promise outlasts the people
themes.body: The first generation dies, but the promise to Abraham does not. Balaam, hired to curse, can only bless, and he declares that God is not a man who changes his mind (23:19). The second census shows a nation still numbering in the hundreds of thousands, and the closing chapters legislate for a land Israel has not yet entered. God's faithfulness, not Israel's, carries the story forward.

themes.title: Leadership and its cost
themes.body: Moses carries the people until he asks to die (11:15), is opposed by his own brother and sister, and finally fails in his own right when he strikes the rock. Leadership in Numbers is burdensome and shared, tested by rivals, and answerable to God. The book ends with the orderly handing on of leadership to Joshua, so that the people will not be left without a shepherd.

keyChapters.why: The first census counts the fighting men of the generation that left Egypt, setting up the contrast with chapter 26 that frames the whole book.
The Nazirite vow and the priestly blessing, one of the oldest and best-loved blessings in the Bible.
The people refuse to enter the land, Moses intercedes by appealing to God's character, and the wilderness sentence is pronounced. The turning point of the book.
Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and Aaron standing between the living and the dead to stop the plague.
Miriam and Aaron die, and Moses, striking the rock in anger, is told he will not bring the people into the land.
The bronze serpent lifted on a pole, which Jesus used to explain his own death in John 3.
Balaam's last oracles, including the star from Jacob and the scepter from Israel, later read as a promise of the Messiah.
The second census: none of the first generation is left except Caleb and Joshua, and a new generation stands ready.

parts.body:
Numbers is the fourth book of the Bible. It has 36 chapters. It tells how Israel traveled from Mount Sinai to the edge of the land God had promised, and why a trip of a few weeks took about forty years.

The book begins with a people counted, ordered and ready. God lives in a tent in the middle of their camp. A cloud leads them by day and fire by night. Then the march begins, and almost at once the people begin to complain: about the food, about Moses, and at last about the promised land itself. When they stand at its border and refuse to go in, God tells them that they will die in the wilderness and that their children will enter instead.

That is the shape of the whole book. One generation comes out of Egypt and dies in the desert. A second generation grows up there and stands at the end of the book on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan River from Jericho, ready to go in.

Numbers is honest about what can happen after a rescue. Freedom from Egypt did not make Israel trusting or grateful. But the book is just as honest about God. He judges, and some of his judgments are hard to read. He also feeds this people every day for forty years, forgives them when Moses pleads, turns a hired curse into a blessing, and brings their children to the border as he said he would. Numbers is about God staying with a people who keep failing.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Numbers is the fourth of the five books of Moses, which Jews call the Torah. In Genesis, God promised Abraham a family, a land, and good for all nations through him. In Exodus, God rescued that family, now a people, from slavery in Egypt, made a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, and had them build a tent, the tabernacle, so that he could live among them. Leviticus gave the laws of offering, priesthood and holiness that let a holy God live in the middle of an unholy people.

Numbers begins one month after the tabernacle was set up. “On the first day of the second month of the second year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt, the LORD spoke to Moses in the Tent of Meeting in the Wilderness of Sinai” (1:1). Israel had been camped at the mountain for about a year. Nineteen days later the cloud lifted and the camp moved out (10:11).

The road was not long. Deuteronomy says in passing that it takes eleven days to go from Horeb, another name for Sinai, to Kadesh-barnea on the southern edge of Canaan (Deuteronomy 1:2). Israel reached Kadesh, sent scouts into the land, and refused to follow them in. After that the book passes over most of the wilderness years in near silence. Deuteronomy counts thirty-eight years from Kadesh to the crossing of the Brook of Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14). The story picks up again in the fortieth year, when Aaron dies on Mount Hor (33:38), and it ends ‘on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho’ (36:13).

So the book moves through three places: the Wilderness of Sinai (1:1 to 10:10), the dry country between Sinai and Canaan with Kadesh as its base (10:11 to 20:21), and the road around Edom to the plains of Moab (20:22 to 36:13). The next book, Deuteronomy, is set on those same plains. It holds Moses' last words to the new generation before he dies. Joshua then tells of the crossing of the Jordan.

parts.h: Why it is called Numbers, and ‘In the wilderness’
parts.body:
The book has two names, and each tells part of the truth about it.

The English name comes through Latin from the old Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, which called the book Arithmoi, ‘numbers’. The name points to the two great counts of the people. In chapter 1 Moses counts the men of fighting age in the generation that left Egypt. In chapter 26 he counts again, on the plains of Moab, and not one man from the first list is left except Caleb and Joshua (26:64-65). The two lists frame the book: one generation gone and another in its place.

The Hebrew name is Bemidbar, ‘in the wilderness’, taken from the book's first sentence. That is where nearly everything happens. The wilderness in Numbers is a real place, dry and dangerous. It is also a time of testing. Moses later told the children of that generation, “Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy 8:2).

A new reader should know that the wilderness is not only a place of punishment. The manna fell every morning of those years. Water came from rock. The cloud never left. The same pages that record Israel's failures record God's daily care.

Numbers names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition has long credited Moses with the five books of the Torah. The book itself says that Moses wrote down the stages of the march at the LORD's command (33:2), and most of it is presented as God's speech to Moses. Readers who hold that Moses is the source of the book's substance generally allow for some later editing. The remark that Moses was ‘a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth’ (12:3) reads more naturally as someone else's comment. The book also quotes older writings, among them a poem from ‘the Book of the Wars of the LORD’ (21:14), which is now lost.

Since the nineteenth century most critical scholars have held that the first five books were woven together from several written strands over a long time. On that view much of Numbers, with its lists and priestly laws, belongs to a priestly source often dated to the exile in Babylon or after it, joined to older stories of the wilderness. These scholars usually date the finished book to the Persian period, after 539 BC, while granting that it holds much older poems, lists and traditions.

When the events took place depends on the date of the exodus, which is debated. An earlier date, about 1446 BC, rests largely on 1 Kings 6:1. A later date, in the thirteenth century BC, rests on the mention of the city Rameses in Exodus 1:11 and on the archaeology of Canaan. Some scholars doubt that the wilderness years can be dated at all.

Two finds bear on the age of the book's material without settling these questions. Two tiny silver scrolls found at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem in 1979, dated to about 600 BC, carry a form of the priests' blessing of 6:24-26. And an inscription in ink on a plastered wall at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, found in 1967 and usually dated to about the eighth century BC, tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor, the same name as the prophet of chapters 22 to 24. Christians who confess the Bible as God's word hold more than one view of how the book came to be. These notes do not settle the question.

Numbers mixes more kinds of writing than any other book of the Torah: lists of names, laws, stories, travel records and poems. A new reader is tempted to skip the lists and laws and read only the stories. It helps to see how the book is laid out, and to notice that the laws are often placed where they answer the story around them.

Chapters 1 to 10 are set at Sinai. The people are counted. The tribes are given their places around the tent, with the Levites nearest. Laws keep the camp fit for God's presence. The priests are given the words of blessing, the leaders bring gifts, the Passover is kept a second time, and silver trumpets are made to signal the march.

Chapters 10 to 12 tell of the first days on the road and the first complaints. Chapters 13 and 14 are the turning point: the scouts, the refusal, and the sentence of forty years.

Chapters 15 to 19 hold more laws and the revolt of Korah. Chapter 15 begins with the words ‘After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home’ (15:2). They come straight after the sentence of death in the desert, and they are a quiet promise that Israel still has a future.

Chapters 20 and 21 carry the people toward Moab. Miriam and Aaron die. Moses himself fails at the rock. Chapters 22 to 25 tell of Balaam, who is hired to curse Israel and can only bless, and then of Israel's fall into idolatry at Peor.

Chapters 26 to 36 belong to the new generation. They are counted, they are given a new leader in Joshua, and they receive laws for a land they do not yet hold. The scholar Dennis Olson, in a study published in 1985, showed how the two counts divide the book into the death of the old generation and the birth of the new.

parts.h: God in the middle of the camp
parts.body:
The first ten chapters can seem dry, but they make one point with great care. Israel is arranged around God. “The Israelites are to camp around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it, each man under his standard, with the banners of his family” (2:2). Three tribes camp on each side. The Levites camp between the tribes and the tent and carry it when the camp moves. God is at the center of the map, and everything else takes its place from him.

The census total is 603,550 men of twenty years and older (1:46). With women and children that would mean two million people or more, and readers have long asked how such a number fits the Sinai desert. Christians read the figure in more than one way. Some take the number as it stands. They note that the tribal totals add up exactly and that God's power is not limited by what seems likely. Others point out that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit, as in Judges 6:15, and that read this way the company would be far smaller. George Mendenhall proposed a form of this reading in 1958. Each reading has its difficulty. The first must explain how so great a number fits what is known of the land. The second must explain why the lists add up as if they were thousands. Christians who hold Scripture as God's word are found on both sides, and these notes take no side. The note on Exodus 12:37 says more.

Because God lives in the camp, the camp must be kept clean (5:3). Chapters 5 and 6 hold laws that follow from this. One of them, the test for a wife whose husband suspects her of adultery (5:11-31), is among the hardest passages in the book for a modern reader, and the chapter note faces it honestly. Another is the vow of the Nazirite, by which an ordinary man or woman could be set apart to God for a time.

Then comes one of the best-loved passages in the Bible. The priests are to bless the people with these words: ‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace’ (6:24-26). God adds, “So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them” (6:27). The blessing is God's own gift. The priests only speak it. It is one of the oldest and best-loved blessings in the Bible, and the silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom show that it was treasured in Jerusalem before the exile.

The section ends with the cloud. When it lifted, the people set out. When it settled, they camped, whether for two days or a month or longer. “They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command” (9:23).

parts.h: The complaints, and the refusal at Kadesh
parts.body:
Soon after the camp leaves Sinai the complaining begins, and it follows a pattern that repeats through the middle of the book. The people complain. God's anger burns. Moses prays. The judgment is stopped or softened. Then it happens again.

In chapter 11 the people weep for the food of Egypt: ‘We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt’ (11:5). The memory is false. In Egypt they were slaves. Moses breaks under the weight and asks to die: “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me” (11:14). God does not rebuke him. He gives him seventy elders to share the load. He also sends quail, and then a plague among those who craved it. In chapter 12 Moses' own sister and brother, Miriam and Aaron, speak against him, and Miriam is struck with a skin disease and kept outside the camp for seven days. That story has sometimes been misused to say things about skin or race or illness. The chapter says none of them, and the note on chapter 12 sets this out.

Then comes Kadesh. Twelve scouts spend forty days in Canaan and come back carrying its fruit. All twelve agree that the land is good. Ten of them say it cannot be taken: “We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!” (13:31). Two, Caleb and Joshua, say that it can, because God is with Israel. The people believe the ten. They weep all night and say, “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt” (14:4).

God's question shows what the refusal was: “How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?” (14:11). The people had not miscounted the enemy. They had decided that God could not be trusted. Moses pleads for them by quoting God's own description of himself, ‘slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion’ (14:18), and God answers, “I have pardoned them as you requested” (14:20). The nation is not destroyed, and the promise stands. But the adults who refused the land will not enter it. They will wander forty years, a year for each day the scouts were gone, and their children, the very children they said would be carried off, will go in (14:31-34).

Pardon and consequence stand side by side here. God forgave, and the refusal still shaped the lives of those who made it. Whether Moses' prayer changed God's mind, or was itself part of God's purpose, is a question Christians answer in different ways, and the chapter note sets them out.

parts.h: Rebellion, priests, and Moses at the rock
parts.body:
The years after Kadesh hold the book's sharpest conflicts over who may lead and who may come near to God.

In chapter 16 a Levite named Korah, with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders, rises against Moses and Aaron. Their claim sounds fair: the whole congregation is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron stand above it? The story treats the claim as a grab for the priesthood. The ground opens under the rebels, and fire burns up the 250. The next day the people blame Moses for the deaths, and a plague breaks out. Aaron takes a censer of incense and runs into the middle of the dying. “He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted” (16:48). The priest the rebels wanted removed is the one who saves them.

These are severe pages, and a reader should feel that. They are told as events at a particular moment in Israel's beginning. They are not offered as a picture of how God deals with every doubt or question, and they give no leader today the right to call a critic a Korah.

Chapter 17 confirms Aaron's priesthood with a sign of life, a dead staff that buds and bears almonds. Chapter 18 sets out the duties and support of priests and Levites. Chapter 19 gives the rite of the red heifer, by which a person made unclean by touching the dead could be made clean again. In a book where a whole generation is dying, that law is a mercy.

In chapter 20 the first generation's leaders reach their end. Miriam dies. The people cry out for water, and God tells Moses to speak to a rock. Moses says, “Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” and strikes it twice (20:10-11). Water pours out. But God says to Moses and Aaron, ‘Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land’ (20:12). Readers have long discussed exactly what the fault was: the striking, the angry words, or the ‘we’. God's own verdict names a failure of trust. Before the chapter ends Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar wears his robes.

Even Moses is not above the book's judgment. And even so, God does not cast him off. He leads the people to the end.

parts.h: The road to Moab: the snake, the wars, Balaam and Peor
parts.body:
Chapter 21 opens with the last complaint of the wilderness and one of the strangest cures in the Bible. The people speak against God and Moses. Venomous snakes come among them, and many die. The people confess, Moses prays, and God says, “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live” (21:8). The snakes are not taken away. A way to live is given, and it works by looking. Jesus later used this very scene to explain his own death (John 3:14-15).

Then Israel fights its first wars east of the Jordan. Sihon, an Amorite king, refuses passage and attacks, and Og of Bashan does the same. Israel defeats both and takes their land. These accounts, and the vow against Arad at the start of the chapter, use the language of total destruction. They belong with the wider question of the conquest, which is taken up below.

Balak, king of Moab, watches all this in fear and hires a famous seer, Balaam, to curse Israel (chapters 22 to 24). The story has humor in it. The seer cannot see the angel that his own donkey sees. Four times Balaam opens his mouth to curse, and four times he blesses. “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind” (23:19). In his last oracle he looks far ahead: “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (24:17). Jewish readers before the time of Jesus read this as a promise of a coming king, and Christians have read it of Christ. The note on chapter 24 sets out both.

All this time Israel knows nothing of it. The people are camped in the valley while their future is fought over on the heights above them, and God guards them without their knowing.

The next chapter is the bitter turn. What a curse could not do from outside, Israel does to itself. At Shittim the men of Israel fall into sexual sin with women of Moab and bow down to their gods, joining in the worship of Baal of Peor (25:1-3). A plague kills twenty-four thousand. It stops when the priest Phinehas kills an Israelite leader and a Midianite woman with a spear. The text praises his zeal. Later readers sometimes took the story as a pattern for violence in God's name, and the New Testament does not. No one may use it that way today.

After the plague comes the second count (chapter 26). The total, 601,730, is almost what it was at Sinai. The promise to Abraham has outlived the people who refused it.

The chapters that follow are full of confidence that Israel will soon live in the land. Five sisters, the daughters of Zelophehad, come before Moses and the whole assembly. Their father died with no son, and by custom his name and land would be lost. They ask for his share. Moses brings their case to God, and God answers, “The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly” (27:7). Their request becomes law for all Israel. The ruling works inside a system in which land passed through sons, and it does not overturn that system. But the book names all five women, three times, and it ends with their story (chapter 36).

Moses, told that he will soon die, asks for one thing: a leader, ‘so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd’ (27:17). God gives Joshua. Chapters 28 to 30 set out the offerings of the year and the rules for vows. The rules about the vows of wives and daughters belong to the households of their world. They are not a rule for any husband's or father's control today.

Chapter 31 is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible. God commands war on Midian for the plot at Peor. The army kills the men. Moses then orders the death of the boys and of every woman who has slept with a man, and the girls are kept alive for the Israelites. That is in the text. It should not be softened, and these notes do not defend what cannot be defended. The chapter note sets out how Christians have read it, and it says what must be said: no one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people.

The last chapters look across the river. Two and a half tribes ask to settle east of the Jordan and promise to fight beside their brothers first (chapter 32). The stages of the forty years are listed (chapter 33). The borders are drawn (chapter 34). Towns are set aside for the Levites, and six of them are cities of refuge, where a person who has killed someone by accident can flee and be heard before anyone takes revenge (chapter 35). The reason given shows how much a human life is worth in this book: ‘bloodshed pollutes the land’ (35:33), and God says, “For I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites” (35:34).

parts.h: The wars and judgments in the book
parts.body:
Numbers has more hard pages than most books of the Bible, and a new reader deserves a plain word about them.

Some are judgments of God on Israel itself: fire at the edge of the camp, plague, the earth opening under Korah, the snakes. Some are wars: against Arad, against Sihon and Og, and against Midian. And near the end God commands Israel to drive out the people of Canaan and destroy their idols (33:50-56).

Christians who receive these books as God's word read the wars in more than one way, as the site's pages on the conquest set out. Some take the accounts as they stand: God, who gives every life, judged particular peoples at one moment in history, after long patience, and never gave this as a general rule. Some note that ancient reports of war, such as the Moabite king Mesha's inscription of the ninth century BC, used sweeping language of total destruction as a common way of describing victory, and read the Bible's language in that light. Some read these texts as God meeting an ancient people within the limits of their world, to be read in the light of Christ; others object that this weakens the authority of Scripture. Each reading has a cost, and the site takes no side among them.

Several things hold on every reading. The book judges Israel by the same standard, and more often. It warns that if Israel takes up the ways of the nations, ‘I will do to you what I had planned to do to them’ (33:56). The commands were tied to one land and one time. They name no modern nation, people or conflict. The New Testament never renews them. Jesus rebuked disciples who wanted to call down fire on a village (Luke 9:54-55). And no one may use any page of this book as a reason for violence against anyone.

A reader who finds these chapters painful is reading them with a conscience the Bible itself formed. Abraham asked God, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25), and he was not rebuked for asking.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Numbers
parts.body:
The New Testament returns to Numbers often, and it draws its own lines from the book.

Jesus draws one himself. Speaking of his death, he said, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life” (John 3:14-15). The people in the desert were dying, God provided the cure, it was lifted up where all could see, and it worked by looking in trust.

Paul retells the wilderness story to the church at Corinth. All Israel had the cloud, the sea, the food and the drink, ‘and that rock was Christ’ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Yet most of them fell. “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Paul's warnings are written to the church. He is not telling Christians to look down on Israel. He is telling people who feel safe to look at themselves: “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

The letter to the Hebrews builds a long warning on Kadesh, using Psalm 95. “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:19). Then it turns the story into a promise: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). The rest Israel refused is still held out. Hebrews, too, is addressed to believers, and its concern is their own hearts.

Other echoes are quieter. Mark says that Jesus saw the crowds ‘like sheep without a shepherd’ (Mark 6:34), the words of Moses' prayer in 27:17. Jude and Peter name Balaam and Korah as warnings to teachers who serve themselves (Jude 1:11; 2 Peter 2:15). And where Israel failed its tests over forty years in the wilderness, the Gospels show Jesus tested for forty days in the wilderness and remaining faithful (Matthew 4:1-2).

One thing must be said plainly. The Bible's own writers, Israelites themselves, recorded these failures for Israel's good, and psalms such as Psalm 78 and Psalm 106 sing of them in worship. The wilderness story is never a reason to blame or despise the Jewish people. The New Testament reads it as a mirror for the church.

Numbers is Israel's Scripture first, and its words are woven into Jewish life. The command to wear tassels on the corners of a garment (15:37-41) became the third paragraph of the Shema, the confession recited morning and evening in Jewish prayer, and Jewish men still wear the tassels. Christians have heard the priests' blessing echoed in the grace and peace with which Paul opens and closes his letters.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read the stories and the laws together. A law often answers the story beside it, as chapter 15 answers chapter 14.

Watch the two generations. Ask of any chapter which generation is on stage, and compare the first count with the second.

Watch Moses pray. Again and again one person stands between a guilty people and what they deserve, and God listens.

Do not make the wilderness smaller than it was. The book does not hide Israel's fear, Moses' exhaustion or the grief of the judgments. It also does not hide the manna on the ground each morning.

And read it as the New Testament does, as a book for people who have been rescued and are not yet home. It asks every generation the question it asked at Kadesh. The land was good, and all twelve scouts said so. The only matter in doubt was whether God could be trusted with what lay ahead.

Quail, then a plague: the craving for Egypt and the judgment that followed.

Pardoned, and still barred from the land. Did Moses change God's mind?

A bronze snake on a pole, and how Jesus reads it in John 3:14-15.
The wars with Sihon and Og, and how Christians read the language of total destruction.
God tells Balaam to go and is then angry that he goes; and a donkey speaks.
A star from Jacob: how Jewish and Christian readers have understood Balaam's oracle.
Phinehas and the spear: why his zeal is no warrant for violence today.
A father or husband may cancel a woman's vow: a law of its world, not a rule for control today.

words.line: ‘In the wilderness’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first sentence (1:1).
‘Numbers’, the name given to the book in the old Greek translation, after the two counts of the people (chapters 1 and 26).
Hebrew for ‘thousand’. It can also mean a clan or a military unit, which is why the census totals are read in more than one way (1:46).
The tabernacle, the tent at the center of the camp where God lived among his people and spoke with Moses (1:1; 2:2).
The tribe set apart to carry and guard the tabernacle. They camped between the tent and the other tribes (1:50-53).
A man or woman set apart to God for a time by a vow: no wine, no cutting of the hair, no contact with the dead (6:1-21).
The sign of God's presence over the tabernacle, cloud by day and the look of fire by night. Israel moved only when it lifted (9:15-23).
The bread God gave each morning in the wilderness. The people grew tired of it and longed for the food of Egypt (11:4-9).
The oasis on the southern edge of Canaan where the scouts reported, the people refused the land, and Miriam died (13:26; 20:1).
‘Quarreling’, the name given to the waters where Israel quarreled with the LORD and Moses struck the rock (20:13).
The name later given to the bronze snake Moses made. It had become an idol, and King Hezekiah broke it up (21:9; 2 Kings 18:4).
The god worshiped at Peor, on the heights above the plains of Moab, where Israel fell into idolatry (25:3).
The redeemer, the nearest relative. In chapter 35 he is the ‘avenger of blood’, and the cities of refuge restrain him (35:12).
One of six towns where a person who had killed someone by accident could flee and be heard before anyone took revenge (35:11).

timeline.what: Texts from Mari in Syria describe the mustering of tribal groups for military service, as the census of chapter 1 does.
The Code of Hammurabi in Babylon sends a wife accused by others to the river ordeal, in which an innocent woman could drown. The rite of Numbers 5 uses nothing that could harm.
The two main dates proposed for the exodus. The wilderness years follow whichever is right.

timeline.when: The second year, second month, first day
timeline.what: At Sinai, a year after leaving Egypt, the LORD commands the first count of the people (1:1).

timeline.when: The second year, second month, twentieth day
timeline.what: The cloud lifts from the tabernacle and Israel sets out from Sinai (10:11).
At Kadesh the scouts return after forty days. The people refuse the land and are sentenced to forty years in the wilderness (13:25; 14:34).
The years of wandering, passed over almost in silence. Deuteronomy counts thirty-eight years from Kadesh to the Brook of Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14).

timeline.when: The fortieth year, fifth month, first day
timeline.what: Aaron dies on Mount Hor, one of the few exact dates in the book (33:38).
Israel camps on the plains of Moab across from Jericho. Balaam blesses, Israel falls at Peor, and the new generation is counted (22:1; 26:63).
Mesha, king of Moab, sets up an inscription crediting his god Chemosh with victories over Israel. It names towns that appear in Numbers 21. It was found at Dhiban in 1868.
An inscription on a plastered wall at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor. It was found in 1967.
Two small silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem carry a form of the priests' blessing of 6:24-26. They were found in 1979.
In the Maccabean revolt the priest Mattathias is compared to Phinehas for his zeal (1 Maccabees 2:26).
Simon bar Kosiba, leader of the second Jewish revolt against Rome, is hailed as Bar Kokhba, which means son of the star, after the oracle of 24:17.
The Mishnah is compiled. It holds a whole tractate on the rite of Numbers 5 and records that the rite had been given up in the first century.
George Mendenhall proposes that elef in the census lists means a military unit, not a thousand.
Dennis Olson publishes The Death of the Old and the Birth of the New, on the two generations that shape the book.

map.title: The land the scouts saw, and where the book ends

places.name: Hebron
places.line: The scouts ‘went up through the Negev and came to Hebron’ (13:22), where Abraham had lived. They saw strong people there and lost heart.

places.name: Jericho
places.line: The book ends with Israel camped ‘in the plains of Moab near the Jordan, across from Jericho’ (22:1). The plains lay east of the river; the town is across it, in Canaan.

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: The river between the camp and the land. The last laws of the book begin, ‘When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan’ (35:10).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The hill country east of the Jordan. The tribes of Reuben and Gad saw that it was good for livestock and asked to settle there (32:1). Drawn roughly.

teaching.mapNote: Only four places are drawn, each one placed elsewhere on this site. Mount Sinai, Kadesh, Mount Hor and most of the camps of chapter 33 are left off, because where they lay is debated or unknown, and no route is drawn, because the way Israel went is not known. Kadesh is often placed at the springs of Ain el-Qudeirat in the northeast of the Sinai Peninsula, south of this map.
